text:
great i was just talking to another claude about those vec3 so good timing There are two pieces of work here. Do them in order:


The split — explode the fillShader.ts god file into one-material-per-file

a shared helpers module, and replace the hardcoded fill_pick dispatcher
with a folder-sweep that auto-generates the registry. This is the enabling
change; do it first and get it green before anything else.



Surface modes — add three ways a material can meet geometry: tile
(repeat, the current behaviour), span (one continuous field stretched
across a large surface), and layer (stack materials with a blend). These
are data on the surface, not new shaders.


If at any point the existing behaviour is unclear or a change would alter how any
current material renders, stop and flag it rather than guessing. The visual
output of every existing material must be byte-for-byte identical after the split
(see "Acceptance" at the end). The split is a reorganisation, not a rewrite.


Why we're doing this (the constraints that shape the how)

Three reasons drive the split, and each one dictates a requirement:


Parallel authoring. We're going to run many agents ("goblins") writing new
materials simultaneously. If materials share one file, simultaneous writes
collide. One-material-per-file makes every author write-isolated — each only
ever creates a new file, never edits a shared one. This is the whole point, so
the design must guarantee no shared file is ever edited to add a material.
Cheap culling. The authoring model is make-many, keep-the-good, delete-the
rest. Deletion has to be free: removing a material must be rm <file> and
nothing else — no dispatcher edit, no ID renumber, no registry hand-edit. If
deletion touches a shared file, the model breaks.
No god files. ~4000 lines of independent fns sharing a preamble is a
directory wearing a trenchcoat. Each material is self-contained
(fn name(uv, px, variant, seed) -> vec3f), references only shared helpers, and
is independently deletable. That's a per-file structure by definition.


The requirement that falls out of all three: the dispatcher cannot be a
hand-maintained central list. It must be generated from whatever material
files exist on disk. Authors declare their material in its own file; a build step
sweeps the folder and generates the registry + dispatch. No central file is ever
touched to add or remove a material.


Part 1 — The split

Target structure

shaders/
  helpers.wgsl          # shared, stable, HAND-OWNED. rand, fbm, snoise, sat, sat3,
                        # line_near, speckle, vertical_drips, blotch, crack_field,
                        # segment_mark, dot_mark, rect_mask, leaf_cover, leaf_color,
                        # paint_window, brick_wall, wallpaper_base, quality_pass, etc.
  materials/
    road.wgsl           # one material per file: exactly one `fn <name>(uv, px,
    concrete.wgsl       #   variant, seed) -> vec3f`, plus a self-describing header.
    brick.wgsl
    blade_steel.wgsl
    ...                 # every current material becomes one file here
  _generated/
    registry.ts         # GENERATED by the folder sweep — do not hand-edit
    dispatch.wgsl       # GENERATED fill_pick equivalent — do not hand-edit
  build-shaders.ts      # the sweep: scan materials/, parse headers, emit _generated/
  index.ts             # assembles helpers + materials + generated dispatch + fs_main

Keep the language as-is (WGSL func bodies). The current files are .ts string
exports; you may keep .wgsl.ts string-export files if that's cleaner for the
existing build — the extension doesn't matter, the one-material-per-file +
generated-dispatch shape does.

Self-describing header (this replaces the dispatcher)

Every material file declares itself in a header comment the sweep can parse.
Minimum fields:

// @material blade_steel
// @board metal_yard          # category/board name (see board list below)
// @variants 3                # how many takes variant 0..N-1 the fn handles
// @author siah               # provenance — goblins stamp their own id
// @kind surface              # surface | composition | gradient  (see modes below)
// @tags metal, weapon, industrial
fn blade_steel(uv: vec2f, px: vec2f, variant: f32, seed: f32) -> vec3f { ... }

The build step (build-shaders.ts) sweeps materials/, parses each header, and
generates:


registry.ts — the typed list of materials (name → board, variant count, kind,
tags, author) that the editor's material browser reads. This is what makes the
Blade Steel-style picker populate; it should be derived, never hand-written.
dispatch.wgsl — the generated fill_pick equivalent. It composes
helpers.wgsl + every materials/*.wgsl body + a generated selection block
that maps a stable material id to its fn call.


Material ids must be stable across builds (deleting one material must not
renumber the others, or saved surfaces that reference material N break). Derive
the id from the material name (e.g. a content hash of the name, or a persisted
name→id map committed alongside — a stable string key is simplest; only convert to
an integer index at the GPU boundary if the D[] contract requires a float). If
you must keep numeric D[0] material ids for the storage buffer, generate a
name→id table in registry.ts and keep it stable (append-only; a deleted
material leaves a tombstoned id that's simply never dispatched). Flag if the D[]
contract makes stable ids awkward — we can widen it.

What must NOT change


Shared helpers stay shared and hand-owned. Do not let materials each carry
their own copy of fbm/rand/line_near/etc. helpers.wgsl is the small
fixed engine; materials are the data that plugs into it. If a material needs a
new general helper, it goes in helpers.wgsl (flag it), not inlined per file.
quality_pass stays central in helpers.wgsl. It's the PSX→Max grade +
per-board grime/bloom branching + the retro dither path. Its per-board branches
currently key off D[4] board — keep that working. If boards become tags
rather than integers, map tag→grade-profile in one place and flag the change.
D[] = [materialId, variant, seed, quality, board] contract and the
fs_main entry (tile-local quantise + vignette + quality_pass) stay intact for
tile mode. Span/layer modes extend this; they don't replace it (Part 2).
The func-library-without-entry-point export (FILL_FUNCS, reused by the
world-scaled atlas painter — "rule of two") must survive: the generated
dispatch.wgsl should still be exportable without fs_main so the atlas
painter keeps reusing the exact same material fns. Do not fork the materials.


Current board list (preserve as categories)

A/Environment, B/Condemned, C/Props, D/NeonRot, E/NeonSurface, F/Contraband,
G/Liminal, H/SecondPass, I/Facades, J/WallProps, K/StreetGround,
L/WoodBrickStone, M/MetalYard, N/Wallpapers, O/Gradients. Every current material
keeps its board as its @board. New materials pick an existing board or propose a
new one in their header (flag new boards so we can bless them).

Deletion contract (verify this works)

After the split, deleting a material is exactly: rm materials/<name>.wgsl
then rebuild. The sweep regenerates registry.ts and dispatch.wgsl without it.
No other file is edited. Confirm this in the acceptance run.


Part 2 — Surface modes: tile / span / layer

These are how a material meets a surface, chosen per-surface as data. None of
them require new material shaders — they're all "feed the existing f(uv) different
UVs, or blend two f(uv) outputs."

Mode 1 — Tile (current behaviour, the default)

Each geometry piece gets local uv = 0..1 and renders the whole pattern, so the
material repeats across a surface. Correct for high-frequency detail materials
(brick, concrete, fabric, metal). This already works; it's the default. seed
still varies per-tile so tiles aren't identical.

Mode 2 — Span (one continuous field across a large surface)

Instead of every piece seeing uv 0..1, each piece sees its slice of a larger
UV space. A wall made of a grid of pieces, spanning a material, reassembles into
one continuous image — e.g. a single vaporwave sunset stretched up the whole
side of a building, not the sunset tiled forty times.

The material fn does not change. The only difference is the UV handed to it:


Tile: piece at grid cell (gx, gy) → uv = fract(local)  (0..1 per piece)
Span: piece at grid cell (gx, gy) in an (W, H) surface →
uv = (vec2f(gx, gy) + local) / vec2f(W, H)  (each piece gets its sub-rect of
the global 0..1)


So "span" = give the geometry a global UV mapping across the whole surface
instead of a per-piece local one. Implement it as a per-surface flag +
the surface's (W, H) extent so the shader/geometry can compute the slice.

Frequency caveat — bake this into guidance, not code: spanning stretches a
material's detail. A material tuned for a 2 m tile looks sparse across 40 m.
Therefore:


Low-frequency / compositional materials span well — gradients, sunsets,
murals, sodium fog, big signage, wall_billboard, all of board O. These want
to span. Mark them @kind gradient (span-friendly).
High-frequency detail materials want to tile — brick, concrete, metal.
Mark them @kind surface (tile by default).
@kind composition = assembles-into-structure pieces (facades, shopfronts) —
usually tiled but edge-aware (see the piece-set note below).


The @kind field lets the editor default the mode correctly (gradient → offer
span; surface → default tile) while still letting the author override per-surface.

Mode 3 — Layer (stack materials with a blend)

A surface carries a base material + zero or more overlay layers. The engine
evaluates the base, then folds each overlay on top via a blend. This is how we get
"brick wall, with a vaporwave sunset washed over it at dusk."

Do NOT implement this by writing combined shaders (brick_vaporwave.wgsl) —
that's an N×M explosion and reintroduces the god-file/coupling problem. Implement
it as a composable layer stack in the surface data:

Surface {
  base:   { material, variant, seed, mode: tile|span }
  layers: [
    { material, variant, seed, mode, blend, factor }   # 0..N overlays
  ]
}

Evaluate: col = base(uv), then for each layer col = blend(col, layer(uv), factor).

Blend modes — keep a small fixed vocabulary (5 max), same discipline as the
door behaviours. These map to one-liners over the two vec3f outputs:


over   — alpha wash: mix(base, over, f)               (flat tint / filter)
add    — light: base + over * f                        (neon glow, sun —
light adds photons, base shows through; this is the right one for
the sunset-glow-over-brick example)
multiply — shadow/grime: mix(base, base*over, f)       (darkening, staining)
screen — bright haze/bloom: 1 - (1-base)*(1-over*f)
mask   — overlay only where a mask says: mix(base, over, f * mask(uv))


The blend factor should be allowed to be a function, not just a constant —
this is what turns a flat filter into believable light:


constant 0.25 → uniform wash (fine, but reads as a filter)
0.30 * uv.y → strong at the top of the wall, fades to nothing at the bottom —
reads as directional sunset light raking down the face
sunset_intensity(U.time) → the overlay ramps 0 → 0.3 → 0 across the day/night
cycle: the wall is plain brick at noon and neon-washed at dusk, same wall,
driven by time. (U.time is already available in the shader — water,
neon_tube, crt_screen use it.)


Support at minimum: constant factor, a uv.y/uv.x gradient factor, and a
U.time-driven factor. A small factor-expression enum (const | gradientY | gradientX | timePulse) parameterised by data is enough — do not embed arbitrary
script; keep it declarative (named factor kinds + params), same rule as the rest
of the engine. Flag if you think we need more factor kinds.

This layer stack is the dual-tone system HMSC wants: the base is what the place
is (grime, brick, rot); the overlay is what the light/mood does to it (neon,
sunset, sodium haze); the blend mode is the physics (add=light, multiply=grime);
the factor is where/when (gradient rake, time-of-day). Any base × any overlay
is expressible as data with zero new shaders.

Note for later (do NOT build now — just don't preclude it)

We also want edge-matched piece-sets — e.g. 20 brick-wall pieces whose edges
line up so they place side-by-side into one long non-repeating wall (kills the
"same stain every 3 m" tell). That's a future @kind composition direction where a
material fn takes edge-phase parameters so its left/right/top/bottom seams match
neighbours. Don't implement it in this pass, but keep the material fn signature
and the surface schema open enough that a future material can receive
neighbour/edge context without a breaking change. Flag if the current signature
would block it.
resolution: Part 1 (the split) done and verified; Part 2 (surface modes) not started this pass. Split cart/hmsc-int/render3d/fillShader.ts (2822 lines, 112 materials across 15 boards) into cart/hmsc-int/render3d/shaders/: helpers.wgsl (18 shared helpers incl. neon_grime, which wasn't in the spec's example list but is used by 8 board-D materials the same way brick_wall/wallpaper_base are), materials/<fn>.wgsl (one file per material, self-describing header: @material/@slug/@name/@board/@variant-labels/@kind/@tags/@author), boards.ts (hand-owned 15-board taxonomy), build-shaders.ts (the v8cli sweep, generates _generated/registry.ts + _generated/dispatch.ts from the materials/ folder + an append-only _generated/ids.json stable-id table), and index.ts (thin assembler preserving the exact FILL_FUNCS/FILL_SHADER export shape). Extraction was script-driven (not hand-transcribed) to guarantee correctness at this scale. Extended the header format beyond the original spec (per the confirmed decision) to also carry display name + 3 variant labels, because game/textures/shaders.ts turned out to have a SECOND hand-maintained registry (FILL_BOARDS, 653 lines) mirroring the WGSL dispatcher's exact order — that's now derived from the generated registry instead of hand-edited, closing the write-isolation gap end to end (CATEGORY_BY_SLUG left as-is, it has a safe default so it doesn't block add/delete). Rewired the 2 real consumers (game/textures/shaders.ts, editors/model/MaterialFill.tsx) to the new module; deleted the superseded fillShader.ts. Verification: independently re-extracted every material body and confirmed byte-for-byte presence in the pre-split committed source; did an order-independent multiset diff of the full assembled FILL_FUNCS against the last-committed fillShader.ts (equal) and confirmed fs_main byte-identical; full esbuild bundle of cart/hmsc-int compiles clean; ran the deletion contract as a live dry run (deleted materials/copper_patina.wgsl, reran build-shaders.ts, confirmed registry.ts/dispatch.ts updated and nothing else needed touching, then restored it and confirmed it got back its exact original stable id from the tombstoned ids.json entry). Landed via another session's consolidation checkpoint (949631487) rather than my own commit — verified the committed tree matches by diffing against it directly. Flagged for review, not blocking: (1) fbm/snoise deliberately omitted from helpers.wgsl since framework/gpu/effect_math.wgsl already auto-prepends them — redefining would be a WGSL duplicate-symbol error; (2) @kind classification (surface/composition/gradient) on ~110 materials was my judgment call per the confirmed rules, worth a skim — board O + sunset_grad + wall_billboard = gradient, board I brick_* = composition, wall_sign left as surface (small 3D prop, not a spanning field) despite being named alongside wall_billboard as signage; (3) docs/game/_index/records/hmsc_int.ts has a narrative mention of fillShader.ts's old path that should get a follow-up docs pass per this repo's maintenance contract, not done here. Part 2 (tile/span/layer surface modes + the blend/factor system) requires first mapping the actual surface/piece data model and UV/D[] construction call sites in hmsc-int's world authoring code, which I haven't explored yet — did not want to guess my way through an unfamiliar subsystem in the same already-large pass. Ready to pick it up next.
